extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners (and patent practitioners evaluating subject-matter eligibility)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea (particularly 'mental processes' and categories like economic, commercial, or interpersonal practices) under §101/Alice step analysis. Focuses on how to identify abstract-idea groupings and apply tests (including consideration of computers/physical aids and claim scope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite fundamental economic practices (e.g., methods for hedging risk, managing financial instruments, or other economic practices) are viewed as reciting an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court determined hedging is a 'fundamental economic practice' and therefore an 'unpatentable abstract idea.' Examples include hedging (Bilski), mitigating settlement risk (Alice/CLS), wagering rules (In re Smith), managing life insurance stable-value policies (Bancorp), offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs.), local processing of payments (Inventor Holdings), using mail markings to communicate sender/recipient/contents (Secured Mail Solutions), and placing orders based on displayed market information (Trading Technologies). The agency treats such economic practices as abstract ideas under step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions — agreements/contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to agreements in the form of contracts or contractual relationships (e.g., transaction performance guaranties) are commercial/legal interactions that can be abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: buySAFE claimed creating a 'transaction performance guaranty' and was described as 'squarely about creating a contractual relationship.' Other contractual examples include managing a stable value protected life insurance policy via calculations (Bancorp) and processing insurance claims under an insurance policy (Accenture/Guidewire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions — legal obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are essentially legal obligations or legal tools (e.g., tax-free exchanges, regulatory/tax structures, hedging) can be abstract ideas as commercial/legal interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Fort Properties claimed aggregating real property and subjecting shares to a master agreement (tax-free exchanges) and was found to be an abstract concept. Other listed legal-obligation examples include hedging (Bilski), mitigating settlement risk (Alice/CLS), and arbitration (In re Comiskey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions — advertising/marketing/sales activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite advertising, marketing, or sales activities or behaviors may be abstract ideas under the commercial/legal interactions grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ultramercial's eleven-step method for displaying an ad in exchange for access (using advertising as an exchange/currency) was held to recite an abstraction. Other examples: structuring a sales force or marketing company (In re Ferguson), algorithms determining optimal business visits (In re Maucorps), and offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions — business relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims describing business relations or interactions between commercial parties (e.g., customer/dealer/financing workflows or clearing-house relationships) can be abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Credit Acceptance (processing a credit application and creating financing packages) was characterized as directed to the abstract idea of processing a financing application. Another example is Dealertrack (processing through a clearing-house between dealers and funding sources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that organize or manage personal behavior, relationships, or interactions (including social activities, teaching, following rules/instructions) fall into an abstract-idea subgrouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include budgeting/tracking spending limits (Intellectual Ventures/Capital One), filtering content (BASCOM — which was found abstract at 2A though 2B reversed), considering historical usage while inputting data (BSG Tech.), neurologist mental processes (In re Meyer), voting/self-verification (Voter Verified), attention managers for non-disruptive information delivery (Interval Licensing), and game rules (In re Marco Guldenaar). The guidance treats 'managing human activity' practices as long-standing human activities that can be abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental processes are concepts that can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper (observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions) and are considered abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities cited: CyberSource, Benson, Mayo, Parker v. Flook. The courts treat methods performable mentally (or by pencil-and-paper) as unpatentable abstract ideas because they are 'basic tools of scientific and technological work.' The guidance emphasizes that 'mental processes' is a type of abstract idea and applies irrespective of statutory claim category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes — A: Limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind do not recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If claim limitations cannot practically be performed in the human mind (the human mind is not equipped to perform them), the claim does not recite a mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify when claimed operations require capabilities beyond human mental performance. Examples: GPS pseudorange calculations to compute absolute position/time (SiRF Tech.), detecting suspicious network activity via monitors/analyzing packets (SRI Int'l), specific multi-step data-encryption methods involving manipulation of data structures (Synopsys), and pixel-by-pixel halftone image rendering using masks (Research Corp.). These demonstrate practical impossibility of human mental performance and thus are not mental-process abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes — B: Claims that encompass a human performing the steps mentally (with or without a physical aid) recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind—either purely mentally or with simple physical aids like pen and paper—it falls within the mental-process grouping (an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of physical aids (pen/paper/slide rule) does not negate the mental nature; it only accounts for differences in memory/capacity. Examples: constructing a map/listing of credit card transactions (CyberSource) could be done by writing down transactions; Benson and Flook noted computations by pencil-and-paper; Univ. of Florida v. GE relied on spec descriptions of pen-and-paper methodologies. Claims that 'read on' a human performing the steps mentally are abstract (see Synopsys, Symantec, Mortgage Grader).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes — C: Claims that require a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that requires a computer can nonetheless be directed to a mental process if the claimed concept could be performed mentally or if the specification describes it as a human-performed concept merely implemented on a generic computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should analyze the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in view of the specification to determine whether the applicant is simply claiming a concept performed on a generic computer or using the computer as a tool. Precedents: Benson (algorithm performed mentally despite being implemented in a computer), Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping could be performed by humans). If the spec describes the concept as human cognitive actions or pen-and-paper methods, the claim may be an abstract mental process even though computer-implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes — C.1: Performing a mental process on a generic computer
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing a mental process on a generic computer does not necessarily render it patent-eligible; claims that are 'human cognitive actions' merely implemented on general-purpose hardware remain abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Voter Verified (voting/verification steps described as human cognitive actions even when performed on a computer), Versata (determining a price implemented using general purpose computer hardware). Examiners should look to whether the specification characterizes the claimed steps as human cognitive tasks merely carried out on generic computing hardware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes — D: Product and process claims may both recite mental processes; 'mental processes' refers to the type of abstract idea, not statutory claim category
rubrics_metrics.description: Both product claims (systems, computer-readable media) and process claims can recite mental-process-type abstract ideas; the courts do not limit the mental-process grouping to process claims only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit has identified numerous product claims (e.g., system and computer-readable media claims in Versata) as reciting mental-process-type abstract ideas. Examiners must apply the mental-process analysis based on the concept recited, not on whether the claim is drafted as a product or a process.
